findings.short_summary: json.dumps oracle can't see tuple vs list
findings.summary: `_dumped`'s `json.dumps` comparison is type-blind, so the oracle cannot assert the tuple-to-list conversion the cases at :412 and :413 exist to cover, nor any container/scalar subclass identity.
findings.failure_scenario: `json.dumps((1.23, 2.35)) == json.dumps([1.23, 2.35]) == '[1.23, 2.35]'`, and `default=str` further collapses anything unserializable to its `str()`. The approved plan's Proof 5 names "a `tuple` (must become a `list`)" as a required case and `_ROUND_FLOATS_CASES` duly carries `(1.23456789, 2.3456789)` and `[(1.23456789,), (2.3456789,)]` — but the comparison function cannot distinguish pass from fail on that property. A later fast-path extension such as `if type(obj) is tuple: return obj` (a tempting next optimization, since tuples currently take the slow ladder) changes `_round_floats`'s return type contract and leaves both oracle tests green. The same blindness covers `_FloatSubclass`/`_IntSubclass`/`_DictSubclass`: `_mishandles_a_dict_subclass` only diverges because its *values* stay unrounded, not because its type differs, so the two-sidedness proof at :463 does not demonstrate type coverage either. (For the record, a type-preserving 40k-case differential fuzz confirms the shipped implementation IS equivalent today — the gap is that the committed oracle would not notice if it stopped being.)

findings.short_summary: docstring wrongly calls the bool guard load-bearing
findings.summary: The new docstring says the `bool` guard 'becomes load-bearing' under the int fast path, but the fast paths dispatch on exact `type()`, so the guard is still completely inert.
findings.failure_scenario: The plan predicted the guard would stop being dead code because the chosen implementation 'does' write an int fast path. It writes an exact-type one: `elif t is str or t is int or t is bool or v is None` (:198, :210). `type(True) is int` is False, so a bool never reaches the int arm — it is copied by the explicit `t is bool` arm — and the fallback ladder still has no int branch. The concrete cost is a reader (or a later refactor) trusting a stated invariant that no code and no test enforces: whoever next simplifies `_round_floats` will read this sentence, believe the guard is protected, and it is not. The plan's own rule — 'no test may claim removing it is observable' — is honoured; the docstring is what breaks it.

findings.failure_scenario: Measured against `build_perf_fixture_db` in the worktree: 548 dates, every one holding exactly 1 activity, all 548 typed `running`, and `avg_pace_sec_per_km` NULL on all 548 (scripts/perf_fixture.py:50-60 makes the paceless-ness deliberate). findings.summary: The new drift-vs-regression rule (3) asserts that one benchmark out of line with its siblings is necessarily a code regression, but three of the five benchmarks pin `today=_TODAY` and two read the real clock, so the two can diverge from the three with no code change at all.
findings.failure_scenario: CLAUDE.md:200-202 now states: 'One benchmark out of line with its four siblings is a code regression however slow the runner was.' In tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py, test_bench_assemble_brief_context (:107), test_bench_build_plan_section (:128) and test_bench_daily_snapshot (:133) all pass `_TODAY.isoformat()` explicitly, while test_bench_get_training_plan_progress (:116) and test_bench_get_training_plan_status (:121) call `handler({})` and window on `date.today()`. The three pinned targets therefore do a fixed amount of work forever; the two unpinned ones do more work every day. findings.short_summary: Oracle payload and counted payload are different payloads
findings.summary: The two equivalence-oracle tests run the handler on an unfrozen clock while the two count tests freeze it at `_TODAY`+58d, so 'the real payload' the oracle proves over is not the payload the counts pin.
findings.failure_scenario: `test_get_training_plan_progress_does_not_double_classify` (line 304) and `..._rounds_without_a_call_per_node` (line 315) both call `_freeze_progress_clock(monkeypatch, _TODAY + timedelta(days=58))` before capturing counts; `test_round_floats_output_is_identical_to_the_pre_inline_implementation` (line 501) and `test_the_round_floats_oracle_can_actually_fail` (line 604's capture) call `_capture_progress_payload` with no freeze at all, so the payload they compare is whatever the real wall-clock date produces (`window_end = today + 7d`, tools.py:3853). Today that happens to be the same window; on any other date it is not. The consequence is that the two halves of the proof — 'output is identical over the real payload' and 'the payload costs 83 calls' — are statements about different objects, and a fast-path bug that only shows up for the rows outside the unfrozen window would be counted but never compared.
